newsitem.title: FRANCE: Talks continue as French truckers turn screw.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue as French truckers turn screw.

text.p: French truckers kept up a crippling six-day-old blockade of some 30 towns on Saturday, turning the screw on the economy to try get bosses to bow to their wage and working conditions demands.
Marathon talks with employers went on into the night in Paris under the chairmanship of a Transport Ministry official but there was little sign of progress.

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike last year which badly hurt his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe called on both sides to end the dispute rapidly because road haulage was crucial to the economy.
Unionists accused employers of failing to negotiate seriously and said the next 48 hours would be crucial.

Haulage companies said they agreed to a truckers' demand to be paid for all working hours, including time spent for loading rather than behind the wheel. But unionists said the concession was not new.
The protests showed the first signs of hurting the economy as tens of thousands of trucks blocked motorways, accesses to some 30 towns and a dozen fuel depots.

The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and Bordeaux, the city where Juppe is the mayor and which has been singled out for the worst blockade.
Paris was barely affected, but truckers started blocking a motorway to the capital's giant wholesale food market in Rungis. Police said food was still getting through.
Unions have said they would blockade Paris only as a last resort and roadblocks 150 km (90 miles) around the capital would be more efficient.

Thousands of foreign truck drivers, mostly British and Spanish forced to drive through France between northern and southgern Europe, were stranded in the roadblocks, sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

French truckers in Bordeaux let tens of exhausted Spanish and Portuguese colleagues through their roadblocks. They warned of a safety problem as the tired truckers embark on the long drive home and advised caution to motorists.

The London Foreign Office ordered consulates in France to help stranded British drivers with money and contacts with home. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with French police in order to be able to claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
Former film star turned animal defenders Brigitte Bardot urged truckers not to let animals starve in the blockade.
The Association of Food Industry said the protests was starting to have serious consequences on the industry's logistics and called for a rapid settlement.
The opposition Socialist Party sided with the truckers, who say they are underpaid and hugely overworked because of cut-throat competition between haulage companies.
It said their demands for wage hikes, shorter working hours and the right to retire at 55 rather than 60 were justified.
"Meeting their demands is in the interest of all motorists," the Socialists said, urging the centre-right government to impose a settlement on haulage bosses.
They called on the government to endorse early retirement for the truckers. Employers have agreed provided the government finance it.
